title: What is Christian nationalism, and how should a Christian think about politics?
description: What Christian nationalism is and is not, how it differs from the love of country Scripture assumes, and how a Christian can think about politics without fusing faith and nation.
askedAs: how should a christian think about politics
short: Love of country isn't the problem. Scripture assumes it. Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray for it, and Jesus wept over Jerusalem while He told the city the truth about itself. Christian nationalism is something else: a fusion of Christian faith and national belonging, held more as identity than as doctrine. It holds that the nation is Christian in a covenant sense, that its real people are Christians, that its laws and symbols should secure that status, and that its decline is a spiritual fall to be reversed by taking power back.

The test is where a person's love of country sits. Can it hear the nation criticized, by Scripture or by its own history, without treating that as an attack on God? Can a believer feel a deeper kinship with a Christian in Nigeria than with a neighbor who shares the flag but not the faith? Israel is the one nation Scripture calls chosen, and Amos told it that the covenant made it more accountable, not less.

The temptation to fuse a political cause with the kingdom of God belongs to no single party. On the right it can fuse faith with the nation; on the left it can make a platform the measure of faithfulness just as easily. A Christian can vote, sing the anthem, and pray for whoever holds office, and still belong first to a people no president will ever govern.
